headline: SW Ledge slack at 10:40: albies stacked tight, bass just starting to commit
subhead: The new moon push is squeezing bait against the Block, and the fleet out of Galilee is finally seeing the fall pattern take shape.
body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge ran 10:40 this morning, and for about twenty minutes on either side of it the rip flattened out enough to see albies working bait right on the surface — nervous water, then boils, then gone. That's been the story all week. The new moon on the 10th put a hard push into every tide cycle since, and the Ledge has been running fast enough that most of the productive fishing is happening in that narrow slack window or on the last hour of the drop, when the current eases enough to hold a jig in the strike zone instead of getting swept off it.

That tidal energy is doing exactly what it's supposed to do this time of year — squeezing bait. Bunker schools are tightening up against Sandy Point and along the beach toward North Light, and the albie and bonito run that's been building off the Block has turned into the real deal. We flagged this last week — said this would be one of the hottest albie zones in the region as the run built out — and that's exactly what's happened. Boats working the rip off Southwest Ledge and the drop-off outside the Ledge are finding albies stacked tight on bait balls, with bonito mixed in on the same pushes, especially in the cleaner water off Clay Head where the current sweeps bait around the point.

The albie program hasn't changed much because it doesn't need to: small metal — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in green machine or bone, and Hogy epoxy jigs — cast into the boil and worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. Speed matters more than color most days. When they're up and showing, a long cast past the school and a retrieve that crosses through the edge, not the middle, keeps you from spooking the whole pod. Bonito are eating the same stuff but tend to want it a hair slower and cleaner, so a small silver Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster in that 1/2-ounce range worked at a steadier pace has been out-producing the frantic retrieve when it's straight bonito on top.

Striped bass are the more interesting story right now because they're not all the way there yet. The bunker are tightening under this new-moon push, same pattern we called last week, but the bass are still in that classic early-fall staging mode — following the bait, flashing under it, not committing the way they will once the moon eases off its high and the tide cycles settle into a rhythm the fish can predict. SW Ledge itself has produced some good fish on the last two hours of the ebb, working live bunker on a fish-finder rig or a bunker spoon trolled slow along the edge where the ledge drops from 20 feet down into the 40s. Nothing huge yet — mostly mid-20s to low-30-inch fish, with a few better ones mixed in on the deepest part of the drop after dark. The overslot and giant class that this rip is known for in October hasn't shown in numbers yet, which tracks — that's usually a late-September into October pattern here, not an early-September one.

Fluke has been the tougher conversation at the dock this week, and there's no point dressing it up. The keeper-grade fish that were around the Ledge and off Sandy Point through August have largely cleared out to deeper, cooler structure, which lines up with what's happening across the whole region right now — bigger fluke pushing toward Nantucket Sound and the Shoals as inshore water sits in the low-to-mid 70s. What's left inshore around Block Island skews short. If you're set on fluke, work the deeper edges outside the harbor mouth in 35 to 50 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, but don't plan a trip around it right now — this is a fish that's already halfway to its winter address.

Bluefish have been the reliable fallback, and a solid one. Snapper blues are thick in the back bays and along the beaches, which is the usual precursor to bigger blues showing in bigger numbers, and there's already been some quality adult activity mixed into the albie blitzes off the Ledge and Clay Head — blues in the 4 to 8-pound range crashing the same bait the albies are working. If you're marking bait and getting cut-off leaders, that's your answer; a short piece of 40-pound fluorocarbon ahead of the jig solves most of it without killing your albie hookup ratio.

Sea bass fishing on the reef structure and rockpiles off the Block has picked up slightly with the cooling trend, though it's a secondary bite right now, not a target-worthy one on its own — worth a few drops on the way back in if you're already out there working bottom in 60 to 90 feet.

Looking at the next few days: expect the albie and bonito pattern to hold, and likely extend, as long as this warm-water edge stays put off the Block — that's been the driver all week and there's no sign of it breaking down yet. The bigger question is the bass. If the tide cycle eases off this new-moon peak the way it typically does heading into the back half of the week, look for stripers to start committing harder to the bunker rather than just shadowing it — that's usually when SW Ledge starts producing the better class of fish on the last two hours of the ebb. Keep Sandy Point and the outside edge of the Ledge in the rotation for that shift. If you've only got one window this week, work the slack tide for albies and bonito, then stick around into the drop for a shot at bass on bunker before the current builds back up.
